items.title: Several Final Fantasy XIV Modding Communities Have Banned Popular NSFW Modder
items.summary: The bans came after modder Noffletoff was credibly accused of participating in graphic discussions of illegal content
items.content:
Several major Final Fantasy XIV modding communities have taken steps to remove the work of a popular not-safe-for-work mod creator after chat logs were exposed in which the modder was seen participating in graphic discussions of illegal material.

Content warning for discussion of child abuse sexual assault material (CSAM)

On YouTube, a user identified as Chunni Doll posted a video alleging that modder Noffletoff, along with several other Final Fantasy XIV players, was engaged in the discussion and sharing of CSAM. The video claims that the chats took place in an invite-only chat room that was part of a larger Matrix server centered on loli/shotacon content. (Sometimes described as an alternative to Discord, Matrix servers are decentralized servers that allow for real-time communication.)

The video was accompanied by a Proton document in which screenshots of the chatlogs are displayed. Kotaku has reviewed the document, and while direct references to victims’ names and explicit descriptions of CSAM content have been censored, the alleged participants can be seen making references to content they’ve watched and potentially sharing content with users on another platform called Session. Matrix administrators were made aware of the server and it was shut down and the alleged participants banned.

Noffletoff is the creator of several paid Final Fantasy XI V body and animation mods that are widely used to create NSFW FFXIV content. As a result of these allegations, numerous FFXIV modding communities are purging his work from their platforms. Additionally, Noffletoff’s Patreon and X account have been deleted.

The Final Fantasy XIV Mod Archive (XMA), one of the largest hosting sites of FFXIV mods, has banned the account associated with Noffletoff. Kotaku has reviewed messages sent in the XMA Discord server confirming Noffletoff’s suspension, a decision announced by a moderator after a user asked what would be done in light of the allegations. “I think it’s reasonable at this point to go ahead and suspend Noff’s account (and have done so),” the post read.

Kotaku has also reviewed messages in Booty Bay, a Discord server associated with pirating FFXIV mods. The moderators of that Discord server have taken similar action, removing his mods from their repositories while banning them from future uploads and banning all discussions related to the allegations against Noffletoff. Snowcloak, a Final Fantasy XIV mod program that allows users to view other players’ mods in game, will block the display of Noffletoff’s mods. “Users attempting to use these mods will receive a warning that the file is blocked,” read a message from a Snowcloak moderator, according to screenshots from the server reviewed by Kotaku .

According to the video, the alleged participants have been reported to authorities. Kotaku has reached out to Square Enix for comment.

Review: FFXIV Is Growing Into a Solid Switch 2 Game
items.summary: Yes, there are times when the Final Fantasy XIV experience still seems not exactly optimal on the Switch 2, but the progress Square Enix is making is great!
items.content:
“A Final Fantasy XIV Switch 2 review over a month after its launch? What took you so long, Jenni?” Well, listen. It’s a big MMORPG, for one. But there’s more to it than that. Any MMO is a living beast. You can’t really judge it immediately. It’s not fair to a team constantly working on launch issues. But now that I have spent over a month messing around with it, the Switch 2 release of FFXIV is shaping up to be a really solid version of the game that could work well as both a primary platform or supplemental secondary way to play.

It’s difficult to even begin to broach the story of FFXIV given the Switch 2 version offers options to be prepared all the way up through the Dawntrail expansion. In short, our avatar is a seemingly ordinary individual and new Adventurer’s Guild member who soon finds themselves connected to the Scions of the Seventh Dawn in the Seventh Umbral Era. They are essentially picked by Hydaelyn. Naturally, this means we are the Warrior of Light and are tasked with protecting Eorzea.

Since this is such a mammoth MMORPG and one we’ve seen since 2013, we’ll focus on the Switch 2-specific elements of FFXIV. First, I’m honestly really impressed with how enjoyable it is in handheld mode and feel like it’s the best way to play. The control scheme works well, with it being easy to target characters, enemies, and in-game elements or use skills. Menus are easier to navigate than I expected, especially with the minus button as a means of shifting through to find what I wanted. I also appreciate just being able to, like, tap on the touchscreen to quickly move through a menu or tap icons in the hotbar. Using the built-in keyboard can be a bit frustrating, as you might expect, and means I couldn’t respond as quickly to folks in-game as I would with a more traditional method.

However, what’s also great is the compatibility. There is mouse and keyboard support with the Switch 2 version of FFXIV. Of course, this is the docked approach. But the Joy-Con 2 mouse support is an option that feels unique compared to the other console releases and works well here.

As for performance, it’s probably what you’d expect from FFXIV on the Switch 2. Especially if you already played other Square Enix games on the system like entries in the FFVII Remake trilogy. It looks really good, but the textures aren’t as intricate or detailed as the PS5 or PC version can be. I’d say it’s probably closer in appearance to the PS4 release. I will say I’ve noticed things are a bit more stable in September 2026 than they were in August 2026, in terms of things like frame rate and even loading. But when there’s a busy part of the city or something like a 24-player Alliance Raid, I did notice it felt like the 30fps might have a few moments where it struggled. But even so, it ran well! I could take part and contribute, not feeling like I couldn’t prepare for telegraphed attacks or as though I was lagging behind compared to other players.

What I will say is that the key to an optimal kind of experience in FFXIV on Switch 2 is customization. Work on keybinding. Get rid of nameplates to help remove the clutter on the screen. Head into display limits to perhaps set things to “normal” to see if that helps with loading. Don’t be afraid to turn off effects, if you’re okay with missing out on those visuals, to help with performance.

Yes, there are times when the Final Fantasy XIV experience still seems not exactly optimal on the Switch 2, but the progress Square Enix is making is great! I’m impressed! Bugs are patched quickly. Seeing stable 30 fps is great. There can still sometimes be some loading issues, and it’s not the easiest version for maintaining conversations due to the keyboard entry system. But considering everything, it’s worth trying if you love the game and I think will prove to be an even more viable option as we see more updates over the rest of 2026.

Final Fantasy XIV is available on the Switch 2, PS4, PS5, Xbox Series X, and PC.

items.title: Final Fantasy XIV’s latest patch basically starts Evercold, but only gives you a short taste
items.content:
I know I said last time we’ve officially entered Evercold, but you can take that statement even more literally with patch 7.56. The MSQ for this patch is short but sweet, taking the Warrior of Light, Alphinaud, and Estinien to the fourth. There, we’re trapped on a deserted island, attacked by some strange machines, and saved by what is no doubt a teaser for the new ranged job to be revealed at the Tokyo Fan Fest. I won’t spoil it here, but it looks cool even if it isn’t exactly what I wanted. (I wanted something using Vanille’s whip staff thing from FFXIII, but maybe next time.) There’s unfortunately no dungeon or trial this time around, just two instanced battles, but both are a good time and interesting enough to engage you. The outfit you get at the end of the MSQ this time is also fantastic, and I’ve been using it as my Beastmaster outfit.

The focus of my time with this patch instead has been squarely on Beastmaster, the new Limited Job. As one of the few who love playing Blue Mage, I was stoked to have something similar again, and it seems a lot more people are enjoying this new job than did Blue Mage. That’s for good reason, as Beastmaster seems to focus way more on solo, open-world content instead of needing to go through party finder to get a group together for a dungeon. There is still some of that here, but most of the monsters you can tame are out in Eorzea.

More than anything, it’s nice to have something to do in these old zones again. I’ve been hunting down monsters to add to my besti-beastiery, fighting random mobs for experience, and running FATEs with other random players. That part alone is a lot of fun, but Beastmaster has its own unique gameplay style unlike any other job, even back when Summoner was actually a pet class. The basic loop for Beastmaster has you summon one of your three chosen monsters, then you and your companion attack an enemy to build up your respective TP bars. Once one of you reaches 100 TP, you can use a special color-coded attack, which will then reset your TP back to 0. Every monster only has one color attack, while you have all four at your disposal. To do some real damage, you need to follow up the first attack with the next in the sequence, shown going clockwise on your job gauge. So if you do a green move, your monster needs to use red, for example. Either one of you can start or end the combo too, but you still need to go in clockwise order to gain any bonus effects.

You’re not just waiting around to build up these combos, as there’s still a lot to consider in the moment-to-moment combat, even if it is overall slower-paced than the typical jobs in the game. When summoning a monster to the field, you gain the One with Nature buff, which allows you to use either Borrow or Tempered Release. Borrow lets you gain a special action based on the monster’s species for the duration they are on the field, while Tempered Release has your monster perform their unique skill. You can only use one per summon, so you need to choose wisely. You might want to borrow a cool dodge move that also grants you evasion up for a bit to dodge some incoming AoEs, or you might want your monster’s special healing skill for some more survivability overall. It’s a cool system even if it’s difficult to keep track of all the moving parts.

That difficult to keep track of theme continues in Beastmaster’s special solo content, the Crucible of the Unbroken. This is something of a rogue-like mode, where you move between spaces on a board game, with each space representing an encounter. You can pick a number of Beasties to join you on a board, but again, only three per battle, and all HP persists between encounters. You need to consider what monsters in your party will do the most damage or be the most survivable, when to use special items that grant healing, revives, or special buffs, and what temporary equipment you want to equip. It’s kind of a lot, but having only gone through the first board so far, it's a lot of fun too.

Overall, I’ve been having a blast with Beastmaster. While it can be a bit tedious to level at times, I’d prefer this be something that lasts me a good long while rather than speeding to the current cap of level 50. This’ll probably hold me over until Evercold at least, which is great because I just got all my other jobs to cap after my raiding group disbanded amicably, and I need things to do. Hope you enjoyed the read, and I’ll see you again next patch.

items.title: Review: Final Fantasy XIV on Nintendo Switch 2 is the best version of the game
items.content:
I have wanted to get back into Final Fantasy XIV for quite some time. I am a massive fan of everything it offers, from the art direction to the scope of the world and adventures that are held within it. I love the way that it handles narrative within the MMO format, and the massive range of locations to visit. I really, really love the music (I went to a FFXIV symphony and everything), and just generally the very Final Fantasy design of it.

Related reading: To think that I played this for the first time way back on the PlayStation 3. My thoughts back then.

But – and it’s a big but – Final Fantasy XIV is a MMO, and MMOs do demand a time commitment, both in terms of the raw hours you plug into it, and the frequency with which you need to play. Take a big break from an MMO, and it just becomes progressively more difficult to step back into.

I tried to get back into FFXIV once when I first picked up the ROG Xbox Ally . The device handled the game just lovely, but I’m not a frequent PC player, and so at some point I put the device down, took a long break, and just… let my subscription slip again.

I am, however, a frequent Nintendo Switch 2 player. By that I mean “daily”. And so now, with the game’s little icon sitting right there on my Switch 2 home screen, I’ve been logging in for at least a little playtime every day. I’ve already made significantly more progress than I did on the ROG.

Final Fantasy XIV plays just lovely on Switch 2, to start with that important point. The console’s screen is just large enough to be able to handle the very busy interface (it’s an MMO, it’s necessary) without distracting from the core action when you want to watch the fireworks. The game’s visual engine is just now ever-so-slightly showing its age with relatively primitive character models and textures – it has been going for something like 13 years at this point – but the art direction is still as stunning as ever, and I’ve loved revisiting my favourite parts of the world from my first playthrough.

Speaking of, I have started a totally fresh character and save file (I wouldn’t even be able to track down my original avatar from a decade ago, if she still exists on servers somewhere, even if I wanted to. I can’t remember my username, password, or the email address it was attached to). I love how it’s possible to play through all the base game and early expansions with NPCs, and not rely on parties of humans for the various dungeons. If you’ve ever played a FFXIV dungeon before, you’ll know that human allies tend to… well, race through it. One of the few unpleasant memories I have from my first playthrough of Final Fantasy XIV was getting to the very final dungeon of the base game and basically missing the whole thing (and being left behind) because I was trying to follow the story. The conclusion to literally dozens of hours of play.

Now, thanks to NPCs, you can enjoy most of the many expansions and all the stories within them at your own pace. And enjoy the typically excellent music, enemy layouts and dungeon design without feeling rushed, too. I even took time to take screenshots, which is one of my favourite ways to log my adventures in this game.

There is a downside, though. Because Square Enix wants to funnel players into the later expansions where, from their perspective, all the value to the players is, they’ve taken steps to streamline the earlier parts of the game, meaning that you accumulate experience points much (much) faster, and have to do far (far) fewer quests along the way. I have been exclusively undertaking the main quest line, with no side quests, let alone grinding, and my avatar is more than twice the minimum recommended level for any given quest or boss battle.

I understand why they did this, because otherwise it would be a truly intimidating, overwhelming task for a completely new player to get up to the newer expansions, but it means that those same players don’t get to spend enough time in parts of the world to really enjoy their contribution to the whole. The major cities are fine, but you’ll fly through little town areas where previously you’d spend a gaming session or two completing all the side quests. They’re barely blips and blink-and-you’ll-miss-them moments now, which really messes with the pacing for what was previously a truly wonderfully paced game that slowly walked you from one wonder to the next.

I don’t necessarily know what the solution is there, though if it were possible, I would have appreciated the option to toggle whether I wanted the accelerating levelling on or not.

Still, that’s my only gripe. The only other minor issue is that, when it comes to the chat, the Switch’s virtual keyboard doesn’t exactly allow for the same typing speed as a proper keyboard. I don’t even know if it’s possible to connect a Bluetooth keyboard to the Switch 2, as I haven’t tried yet, but even if it were possible, that would significantly undermine the portability of the experience. Currently I haven’t been social enough in FFXIV to require the chat function much, but I can see that becoming an issue later on in the game.

Those are only minor quibbles, obviously, set against a game that is hundreds upon hundreds of hours in scope, and now in an extremely portable and accessible format. FFXIV is a hobby all by itself, and now I can embrace and indulge it in full.
